title: Buzz self-hosted release manifest
description: Describes one candidate for the private Buzz deployment. Sibling of .release/desktop-candidate.json: same 'schema' integer discipline, same rule that the document is a statement of fact about artifacts that already exist, never a request to go build or fetch something. Prose lives in scripts/selfhost/release-manifest.md; policy lives in docs/selfhost-releases.md. The normative validator is scripts/selfhost/mint-manifest.py, which reads THIS file so the two can never drift.

schema.description: Manifest format version. Bump only for incompatible changes; the deployer refuses anything it was not written against, because a deployer that guesses at an unknown field is a deployer that installs the wrong binary.

name.description: Release label. Deliberately narrow: this string becomes a Docker tag component, a backup directory name, an inbox directory name and part of a rollback binary's filename. Anything that could be read as a path separator, a shell metacharacter or a tag delimiter is rejected here rather than sanitised at four downstream call sites.

source_commit.description: Full 40-hex commit the artifacts were built from. The deployer refuses to run unless the build repo's HEAD equals this, so a manifest can never be paired with a tree it does not describe.

previous_commit.description: Commit believed to be live when the manifest was minted. Advisory only: the deployer re-derives the live commit from the running BUZZ_IMAGE tag at preflight time, because the box is the authority on what the box is running.

created_at.description: UTC ISO-8601 mint time. Advisory; nothing gates on it.

components.description: What this release replaces. A subset: a relay-only or an agent-only release is a normal, encouraged shape, because the smallest change that fixes the problem is the safest change to ship.

image.description: Tag written into /opt/buzz/relay/.env as BUZZ_IMAGE. Restricted to the buzz-local: namespace on purpose: a registry-qualified tag would invite the deployer to pull, and the deployer never reaches the network for artifacts.

image_id.description: Docker's content id for that tag (docker image inspect --format '{{.Id}}'). A tag is a mutable pointer; this is the identity. The deployer refuses if the tag resolves to a different id than the one that was tested.

acp.description: The buzz-acp agent binary, installed to /opt/buzz/bin/buzz-acp (root-owned) and picked up by buzz-claude.service and buzz-codex.service on restart.

cli.description: The buzz CLI, installed to /opt/buzz/bin/buzz (hermes-owned). No service restart: the next invocation gets the new binary.

deploy_order.description: Exact order the deployer walks components. Must be a permutation of the keys of `components` — not a subset, not a superset. If relay-image is present it must come first: the relay is the leg every other component stands on, so it moves first and is proven healthy before anything else moves.

migrations.description: Classification of the migrations/ delta between the live commit and source_commit. `none`: the delta is empty — the schema-neutral fast lane, and the only class an unattended inbox drop may carry. `backward-safe`: the delta is non-empty and every migration in it is expand-only, so the previous binary still runs against the new schema and a binary rollback is clean. `ack-required`: the delta is non-empty and contains at least one change the previous binary cannot tolerate — rollback will not restore service without a database restore. The classification is a human judgement about SQL; nothing auto-derives it, and the deployer only ever checks that the manifest does not UNDERSTATE what git actually shows.

promoted_by.description: WHO APPROVED THIS RELEASE — the coordinates of an owner authorization the deployer re-derives from the relay. Not the authorization itself: a signature copied into a manifest proves only that whoever wrote the manifest could copy a signature, and re-checking it locally would re-check the manifest against itself. These three fields name a question instead — `buzz projects release-check --root <root> --revision <revision> --owner <owner>` — and the deployer asks it of the live relay, requiring exit 0 AND a verdict whose `commit` equals this manifest's source_commit. That last equality is what stops an approval of one commit authorising a release of another. Null means nobody has approved this release: the deployer refuses it outright in inbox mode (an unattended deploy needs the whole ceremony) and requires --allow-unattributed from a human otherwise. Null is still allowed because a hand-driven emergency deploy is a real thing that should be loud rather than impossible.

root.description: The pull-request root event the approval lives on.

revision.description: The revision being released — a 1619 update event id, or the root's own id for a release cut before the first revision.

owner.description: The pubkey whose approval counts. Supplied here rather than discovered, because 'whose approval counts' is a policy the release states and the verifier checks, not something a relay query can answer.

staging_stamp.description: WHAT THE GATES FOUND — a summary of the promotion stamp (`buzz.staging.promote-stamp/v1`, written by scripts/selfhost/gates/stamp.sh) that this candidate earned. Deliberately a SIBLING of promoted_by and never a substitute for it: 'the gates passed' and 'a human with a key approved this' are different claims, and collapsing them is how an audit log starts lying about which one was actually made. Optional — a manifest may carry neither, either or both — but the deployer requires it in inbox mode. This object is a summary, not the evidence: the stamp file itself is staged into the release drop as `promote-stamp.json` beside manifest.json, and the deployer re-hashes it against stamp_sha256 and re-derives every join before believing any of this. A fixed filename, not a path in the manifest, for the same reason install paths are not in the manifest.

stamp_sha256.description: SHA-256 of the stamp file as staged. The binding between this summary and the evidence it summarises; without it the summary is just a claim the manifest makes about itself.

verdict.description: The stamp's verdict, restricted here to the two the gates call promotable. `blocked`, `refused` and `incomplete` are not minted at all — a release built on failed evidence is refused where it is authored, not where it is deployed. `promotable_with_waivers` is NOT equal to `promotable`: a human decided some red tests do not block, and the deployer requires --ack-waivers on the command line before it will ship one.

stamped_at.description: The stamp's own UTC timestamp, copied through. Advisory: nothing expires a stamp today, and pretending a duration is enforced would be worse than not stating one.

waived.description: How many waived test failures were in force, summed across gates[].details.waivers.applied. Zero exactly when the verdict is `promotable` — the minter refuses a stamp where those two disagree, because one of them has been edited.

notes.description: Free text for the human reading the journal at 3am. What changed, what to watch, what to do if it goes wrong. May be empty, but an empty notes field on a migration-bearing release is a smell.

artifact.description: Path to the built binary, relative to the artifact root (which defaults to the directory holding the manifest). Relative and traversal-free by construction — see the pattern and the `not` clause. The deployer runs as root; an absolute path or a `..` here would let a manifest author choose which file root copies, which is the whole ballgame.

sha256.description: SHA-256 of the artifact. Verified at preflight and AGAIN immediately before install, because the interesting window is between those two moments.

bytes.description: Artifact size. Used for the free-space preflight and as a cheap mismatch tripwire before the expensive hash.
